chapterName: Empire: Roman Art and Architecture (c. 500 BC-AD 476)

briefing.title: Rome, AD 113
paragraphs: It is AD 113, and Rome rules the Mediterranean world. In the capital, the emperor Trajan dedicates a towering column carved with his wars in Dacia, while concrete domes, marble-faced forums, steaming public baths and the vast Colosseum crowd the skyline.

Roman art began by borrowing from the Etruscans and the Greeks, but the Romans made it their own: honest portraits of ancestors, painted walls, and engineering that carried water and roads across an empire. Yet tastes keep shifting, and within two centuries a new style will rise.

timelines.name: Level 1: Milestones of Roman Art
timelines.blurb: Four big moments, from the Republic to Constantine.

events.label: The Roman Republic begins
events.fact: The Republic (res publica), the era of elected government, prized portraits that showed men wrinkled and rugged.

events.label: Romans sack Corinth
events.fact: After the sack of this wealthy Greek city, many Greek artists were carried off to Rome as slaves.

events.label: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
events.fact: The eruption's ash preserved the decorated rooms of Pompeii and Herculaneum on the Bay of Naples.

events.label: Arch of Constantine completed
events.fact: The arch mixes older classical roundels with new panels of squat, hard-edged figures.

timelines.name: Level 2: Building an Empire
timelines.blurb: From the first aqueduct to a new style of sculpture.

events.label: Rome's first aqueduct feeds a fountain
events.fact: Rome's first aqueduct supplied a fountain at the cattle market; by the 3rd century AD the city had eleven.

events.label: Earliest known Roman concrete at Cosa
events.fact: Cosa, a colony on the coast north of Rome, has the earliest known Roman use of concrete.

events.label: Colosseum completed
events.fact: The Colosseum held over 50,000 spectators and even staged mock sea battles.

events.label: Trajan becomes emperor
events.fact: Trajan, the soldier-emperor, expanded the empire to its greatest size.

events.label: Hadrian succeeds Trajan
events.fact: Hadrian, a passionate builder, rebuilt the Pantheon in its present form.

events.label: Sculpture turns stumpy and large-eyed
events.fact: Artists abandoned the graceful classical style for rigidly frontal figures, and historians still debate why.

timelines.name: Level 3: Five Centuries of Building
timelines.blurb: Roads, basilicas, emperors and statues in order.

events.label: Romans begin building roads
events.fact: Roads moved armies, officials and trade; at their peak 29 great highways radiated from Rome.

events.label: Oldest known basilica built
events.fact: Basilicas were large halls for business and law cases; Christians later adopted the shape for churches.

events.label: Greek artists enslaved after Corinth
events.fact: By this time most sculptors working in Rome were Greek, and their names were rarely recorded.

events.label: Augustus becomes first emperor
events.fact: Augustus boasted he had found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.

events.label: Ash buries Herculaneum
events.fact: Mount Vesuvius preserved wall paintings in Herculaneum and Pompeii, wealthy towns on the Bay of Naples.

events.label: Trajan's Column dedicated
events.fact: Its spiralling band of carvings shows more than 2,500 figures from Trajan's wars in Dacia, modern Romania.

events.label: Tetrarchs statue group carved
events.fact: This group of four co-ruling emperors, now in Venice, shows the blocky late Roman look.

events.label: Arch of Constantine completed
events.fact: Built near the Colosseum for Constantine, it sets classical carvings beside squat new figures.

trueFalseDecks.name: Borrowers and Builders
trueFalseDecks.blurb: From Greek roots to the city of marble.

cards.claim: After the sack of Corinth in 146 BC, many Greek artists were carried off as slaves.
cards.why: Corinth was a wealthy Greek city, and by the 2nd century BC most sculptors working in Rome were Greek.

cards.claim: Roman artists were celebrated masters who usually signed their works.
cards.why: Roman artists were mostly anonymous tradesmen, and almost no signed works survive.

cards.claim: Under the Republic, it was a mark of good character for portraits to show physical flaws.
cards.why: Republican men were shown wrinkled and rugged, unconcerned with vanity.

cards.claim: Augustus preferred rugged portraits that showed every wrinkle.
cards.why: Augustus preferred portraits that were Greek in flavour and highly idealised.

cards.claim: Most surviving Roman painting was done on wooden panels.
cards.why: Panel painting was the most prestigious, but wood rots; what survives is mostly wall painting.

cards.claim: Pozzolana, a volcanic ash, made Roman concrete unusually strong.
cards.why: Roman concrete mixed lime mortar, water and rubble with pozzolana.

cards.claim: The Romans borrowed the arch from the Egyptians.
cards.why: The arch was borrowed from Rome's Etruscan neighbours.

cards.claim: Christians adopted the shape of the basilica for their first great churches.
cards.why: Basilicas were large halls for business and law cases; the oldest known was built in 184 BC.

trueFalseDecks.name: Arenas, Domes and Aqueducts
trueFalseDecks.blurb: The empire at its grandest, and how its style changed.

cards.why: Completed around AD 80, it also had retractable awnings for shade.

cards.claim: In Roman apartment blocks, the cheapest rooms were on the ground floor.
cards.why: The cheapest rooms were at the top, furthest from water and escape.

cards.claim: In the early 4th century AD, Rome had far more apartment blocks than private town houses.
cards.why: Rome had 44,850 apartment blocks (insulae) against 1,781 town houses (domus).

cards.claim: Trajan's Column tells the story of his wars in Gaul.
cards.why: The column tells of Trajan's wars in Dacia, modern Romania.

cards.claim: The height of the Pantheon's ceiling exactly equals its interior radius.
cards.why: This makes the dome a perfect half-sphere, a size not surpassed until steel frames arrived in the late 19th century.

cards.claim: Most of the water carried by Rome's aqueducts went to private homes.
cards.why: Most of the water went to the public baths.

cards.claim: Trajan's bridge over the Danube was the longest arch bridge for a thousand years.
cards.why: Roman bridges were the first large, lasting bridges ever built.

cards.claim: The statue group of the four Tetrarchs is now in Rome.
cards.why: The Tetrarchs group, carved around AD 305, is now in Venice.

oddOneOut.why: The amphitheatre, basilica and triumphal arch were building types the Romans invented; temples followed an Etruscan layout with Greek column styles.
Three belong to Trajan; the Pantheon was rebuilt by his successor Hadrian.
Lime mortar, rubble and pozzolana went into Roman concrete; thin marble slabs were only a facing on the finished wall.
Stumpy, large-eyed, frontal figures mark 3rd-century AD sculpture; graceful lifelike bodies belong to the classical style it abandoned.
Landscapes, still lifes and Odyssey scenes appear on the walls of Pompeii; mummy portraits are panel paintings from the Fayum in Egypt.
The Pont du Gard, the Segovia aqueduct and the Pantheon still stand; none of the ancestral funeral masks survives.

whoAmI.name: Emperors Who Built Rome
whoAmI.blurb: Three emperors who left their mark in stone.

people.name: Augustus
clues: Under me the quarries at Carrara were opened up for the capital.
I added my own grand forum beside Rome's original Forum.
My portraits were Greek in flavour and highly idealised, and my face spread on coins.
As Rome's first emperor, I boasted I found Rome brick and left it marble.

people.name: Trajan
clues: My bridge over the Danube was the longest arch bridge for a thousand years.
I reigned from AD 98 to 117.
A column dedicated in AD 113 shows my wars in Dacia with over 2,500 figures.
I was the soldier-emperor who expanded the empire to its greatest size.

people.name: Hadrian
clues: I reigned from AD 117 to 138.
I succeeded the soldier-emperor and was a passionate builder.
My temple to all the gods is crowned by a concrete dome with an open 'eye'.
I rebuilt the Pantheon in its present form.

whoAmI.name: Rulers and Writers
whoAmI.blurb: An emperor of a new age and two writers who explained Roman art.

people.name: Constantine
clues: A colossal statue of me now survives only in giant fragments.
My arch near the Colosseum mixes classical roundels with squat new figures.
I moved the capital to the city on the Bosporus once called Byzantium.
Christianity triumphed under my rule.

people.name: Vitruvius
clues: My subject included concrete, the arch, vaults and domes.
I was a working architect of the 1st century BC.
My handbook describes most Roman building techniques.
Mine is the only Roman book on architecture to survive.
reviewFlags: "Vitruvius" appears fewer than 2 times in the chapter

people.name: Pliny the Elder
clues: I believed painting in my day had declined through laziness.
I grumbled that true portrait painting had died out.
I compiled an encyclopedia rather than a building manual.
My encyclopedia is our main ancient source on Roman art.
reviewFlags: "Pliny the Elder" appears fewer than 2 times in the chapter
fact-check: The first clue overgeneralizes: the chapter says Pliny thought true portrait painting had died out through laziness, not that painting in general had declined.

places.name: Corinth
places.why: After Rome sacked this wealthy Greek city in 146 BC, many Greek artists were carried off as slaves.

places.name: Pompeii
places.why: Ash from Vesuvius in AD 79 preserved its painted walls, our main surviving Roman paintings.

places.name: Fayum
places.why: This farming region of Roman Egypt preserved rare realistic panel portraits attached to mummies.

places.name: Cosa
places.why: This coastal colony north of Rome has the earliest known Roman use of concrete, some time after 273 BC.

places.name: Carrara
places.why: Its marble quarries in northern Italy were opened up for the capital under Augustus.

places.name: Pont du Gard
places.why: This aqueduct bridge in southern France still stands as proof of Roman engineering.

places.name: Constantinople
places.why: Constantine moved the capital to this city on the Bosporus, where Roman art grew into the Byzantine style.
